en.title: Afghanistan after the aid-state: territorial consolidation, fiscal recomposition and the social limits of post-2021 stabilization
en.deck: Five years after the Taliban takeover, Afghanistan combines stronger territorial control and domestic revenue collection with falling per-capita income, shallow finance, mass returns, restricted female education and employment, and growing dependence on regional corridors.
en.regime: Post-2021 low-income consolidation: stronger territorial control and domestic revenue coexist with weak per-capita growth, shallow formal finance, constrained human capital and heavy exposure to regional corridors and aid retrenchment.
en.key_risk: The current equilibrium can preserve administrative control while living standards and productive capacity deteriorate if returnee pressure, aid cuts, border disruption, climate stress and human-capital losses outpace private investment.

pt-BR.title: Afeganistão após o Estado financiado por ajuda: consolidação territorial, recomposição fiscal e os limites sociais da estabilização pós-2021
pt-BR.deck: Cinco anos após a tomada de poder pelo Talibã, o Afeganistão combina maior controle territorial e arrecadação doméstica com queda da renda per capita, finanças rasas, retornos em massa, restrições à educação e ao trabalho feminino e dependência crescente de corredores regionais.
pt-BR.regime: Consolidação de baixa renda pós-2021: maior controle territorial e receita doméstica coexistem com crescimento per capita fraco, finanças formais rasas, capital humano restringido e forte exposição a corredores regionais e retração da ajuda.
pt-BR.key_risk: O equilíbrio atual pode preservar controle administrativo enquanto padrão de vida e capacidade produtiva se deterioram se pressão dos retornados, cortes de ajuda, interrupções fronteiriças, estresse climático e perdas de capital humano superarem o investimento privado.

key_constraints: No recent comprehensive census and rapidly changing population estimates due to mass returns
Shallow formal finance and incomplete international banking connectivity
Reduced external assistance and humanitarian funding
Restrictions on female secondary, higher education and employment that weaken human-capital formation
Dependence on regional trade corridors vulnerable to political and border disruption
Limited transparency and comparability of fiscal, security and illicit-economy statistics
selection_rationale: Afghanistan is undergoing a consequential post-2021 state transformation: an externally financed republic and security state has been replaced by a smaller de facto order with stronger domestic revenue collection and territorial control but weaker formal finance, lower external assistance, severe human-capital restrictions and rapidly changing regional trade dependencies. The transition links institutions, security, migration, fiscal capacity, productive structure and regional infrastructure, with consequences that extend across South and Central Asia.
contrary_evidence: Stronger revenue collection, territorial control and aggregate GDP growth provide evidence of administrative stabilization, but falling per-capita income and high subsistence insecurity contradict a simple recovery thesis.

The collapse in opium cultivation demonstrates unusually strong enforcement capacity, but lower farmer income, fallow land and synthetic-drug trafficking weaken the case that narcotics suppression has already become a sustainable rural transition.
Trade rerouting and projects such as CASA-1000 show functional regional integration, but banking isolation, expensive logistics and limited recognition continue to constrain long-horizon investment.

Nationwide conventional warfare has declined sharply relative to the pre-2021 period, while ISIL-K attacks, explosive remnants, rights violations and Afghanistan-Pakistan hostilities preserve significant security risk.
limitations: Afghanistan has no recent comprehensive census; population estimates differ across institutions and are changing rapidly because of return migration.
World Bank and UNDP growth estimates use different periods, data vintages and methodologies and must not be merged into a single time series.
Public fiscal and security data are less transparent and independently auditable than in a normal statistical system.
Large infrastructure and mining projects are assessed by documented implementation milestones; announcements, geological potential and memoranda are not treated as realized productive capacity.
